notes: Check batch: four runs (haiku-1, haiku-2, sonnet-1, sonnet-2), no opus, so opus is unavailable in per_rule. All four have rc 0. result.json gives head 05babfa with uncommitted true and skill_hash 2a2364f71bf17ac763a516ffe91271f19ac36fbf95f543a5910881feac8e2b6e, which equals evals/tools/common.py folder_hash of the working tree's idiomatic-elixir/, so the runs read the current text. git diff 05babfa -- idiomatic-elixir/ touches only the do: rule in SKILL.md: one sentence on if added at its end, and an if Instead-of/write pair added to its example. git diff 0397dec -- idiomatic-elixir/ adds to that the check-4 rewording of the same rule's wrapped-line sentence and the test-name paragraph of references/testing.md, which no macro-dsl rule covers.

Unchanged rules: macros.md and library-design.md are unchanged since 0397dec, so the seven macro and library rules are graded to the standard of sweeps/2026-10-22-b/grades/macro-dsl-skill.json and sweeps/2026-10-22-check-4/grades/macro-dsl-skill.json. Under that standard a direct attribute write inside get's quote counts against Keep quote blocks small, but validation in the macro body outside quote does not. __using__ and __before_compile__ without @doc false are accepted because their __ names hide them (Code.fetch_docs reports :hidden). `if not ... raise` validation is not counted under the branching rule. A one-line multi-step pipeline is listed under the pipeline rule. String.to_atom on route text from source code is not counted under the atom rule.

Changed rule, graded against its current text in idiomatic-elixir/SKILL.md (Readability): Use `do:` for a one-expression body and `do ... end` for anything else. The new sentence is "The same holds for `if`: `if ..., do: ..., else: ...` fits when each branch is one short expression on the `if`'s line, and a branch `mix format` moves onto its own line gets `do ... end`." It decides no verdict here: no run writes `if ..., do:`. Violating runs out of four, per sentence, counted as in check-4:
- "Use `do:` for a body of one expression that reads as part of the head": 0 of 4.
- "A body with several steps, a `case` or `with`, or a comment gets `do ... end`.": 1 of 4. haiku-2 line 92 is `defp parse(path), do: path |> split() |> Enum.map(&parse_segment/1)`, a two-step pipeline on do:. That is the shape of the rule's own Instead-of `def decode(value), do: value |> Decoder.decode() |> normalize_result()`, counted the same way as 2026-10-22-b baseline-sonnet-2.
- "A function whose clauses are short pattern matches keeps them on `do:` even when one clause needs a block; set that clause apart with a blank line.": blank-line part 0 of 4. Keep-on-do: part 1 of 4 as a judgement call that decides no verdict, as at check-3: sonnet-1 writes validate_handler!/1's :ok clause (lines 92-94) as a block, although only the raise clause needs one, and its do: form would be the guard-wrapped head the rule keeps.
- "When most of a function's clauses need blocks, write all of them as blocks.": 0 of 4. sonnet-2's __define__/3 has two of three clauses needing blocks and writes all three as blocks.
- "A `do:` body belongs on the head's line ... write a block or move part of the body into a helper.": 0 of 4.
- "The one wrap to keep is a head that `mix format` breaks after a long guard, with `do:` on the next line.": no guard-wrapped do: line in any file. sonnet-2's __define__/3 lines 70-71 is a head broken after a long guard, but with a do ... end block.
- "The same holds for `if` ..." (new): 0 of 4. haiku-1 and haiku-2 each write two validation ifs, all as do ... end blocks. Rewritten as `if ..., do: raise(...)` and run through Code.format_string!, mix format moves every branch onto its own line: haiku-1 lines 68 and 73 at 126 and 171 characters joined, haiku-2 lines 53 and 57 at 106 and 151. So the blocks are what the sentence asks for. The sonnet runs have no if (they validate with guard clauses).
- Any sentence: 1 of 4 (haiku-2). Haiku is violated and Sonnet clean. check-4 had 0 of 4, and 2026-10-22-b's skill runs had 2 of 5.

Every do: body that mix format leaves on a line of its own, on a function or an if, quoted: none in any of the four files (grep for lines starting with do: or else: finds nothing). No head in the four files has a long guard with a do: body; the only guard-wrapped head is sonnet-2 lines 70-71, `def __define__(module, path, handler)` / `when is_binary(path) and is_atom(handler) and handler not in [nil, true, false] do`, a block. All four runs' last Write calls match their final files except for parentheses that mix format added to the two get calls in MyApp.Router, so no wrapped do: line was written and then reformatted either. The one if do: wrap at check-4 (haiku-2 there) does not recur.

One-expression blocks measured: each block clause's body was rewritten as a do: line and run through Code.format_string!. The segment matcher has four clauses in all four runs: two short do: clauses and two recursive block clauses, each set apart with blank lines. Every recursive clause wraps under do:: haiku-1 match_segments/3 at 145 and 117 characters, haiku-2 bind/3 at 126 and 99, sonnet-1 and sonnet-2 match_segments/3 at 141 and 117. So two of four clauses need blocks, which is not most, and the mixed form is clean everywhere, as in check-4. sonnet-1 validate_path!/1: the raise clause would be 107 characters and wrap, so it is one block clause set apart. sonnet-2 __define__/3: the raise clauses would be 146 and 132 characters and wrap; the first clause would be a guard-wrapped do: of 191 characters joined.

Compile-time dependencies were checked with mix xref trace, one scratch Mix project per run: the run's file copied unchanged to lib/tiny_router.ex, plus real MyApp.PageHandler and MyApp.UserHandler modules in lib/handlers.ex. haiku-1 and haiku-2 never expand the handler. They pass the alias into __put_route__/3 or __define__/3, which runs in the router's module body, so xref reports alias MyApp.PageHandler (compile) (haiku-1 line 115, haiku-2 line 117). sonnet-1 uses Macro.expand_literals with function {:__route__, 0} and sonnet-2 with {:routes, 0}; both report (runtime). That is the same split as check-4 except haiku-1, which used Macro.expand_literals there.

Bad-declaration checks: each run's project was loaded, then Code.compile_string compiled one router declaring get 123, MyApp.PageHandler and one declaring get "/", "not a module". All eight fail with ArgumentError while the router compiles, raised from the @doc false function get's quote calls. haiku-1's messages are prefixed with the module name. All four compile under mix compile --warnings-as-errors and pass mix format --check-formatted; they wrote get "/" without parentheses and mix format added them. Smoke test: all four return routes in declaration order, match "/", "/users/42" and "/users/42/", return :error for "/nope", and raise FunctionClauseError on match(123). haiku-2 returns atom param keys (%{id: "42"}); the other three return string keys.
Reads: all four read SKILL.md, macros.md and library-design.md with one Read call per file before writing tiny_router.ex. That matches result.json reads and satisfies the Expected reads line.

Against check-4: the do: rule moves from clean to violated on Haiku, through a two-step pipeline on a do: line (haiku-2), not through a wrapped line. The compile-time-dependency rule is again violated on Haiku, now by both runs, and stays clean on Sonnet. The other six rules stay clean on both tiers. Both haiku runs write the one-line three-step pipeline in __before_compile__; both sonnet runs split it over lines.

Use `do:` for a one-expression body and.evidence: line 97: defp match_segments([], [], params), do: {:ok, params}; line 99: defp match_segments([":" <> name | routes], [segment | segments], params) do; line 103: defp match_segments([segment | routes], [segment | segments], params) do; line 107: defp match_segments(_routes, _segments, _params), do: :error. Lines 68-71: if not is_binary(path) do / raise ArgumentError, / ... / end and lines 73-76 are if blocks whose do: forms mix format would move onto their own lines (126 and 171 characters joined). No do: body is wrapped onto a line of its own, on a function or an if, and no head is guard-wrapped.
